concepts.definition: The 10-yard area at each end of the field. Get the ball into the other team's end zone and it is a touchdown.
concepts.exampleLine: He got both feet in the end zone. Six points.

concepts.definition: The imaginary line where the ball sits before each play. Nobody may cross it before the snap.
concepts.exampleLine: Their guy jumped over the line of scrimmage. Flag.

concepts.definition: Where the ball sits on the 100-yard field. The closer to the other end zone, the fewer yards you need to score.
concepts.exampleLine: Starting at midfield is a gift.

concepts.definition: The offense gets four plays (downs) to gain 10 yards. Gain them and the count resets to first down.
concepts.exampleLine: They have to go for it on fourth down.

concepts.definition: The yellow line on TV and the orange pylon-and-chain on the field that show where 10 yards ends.
concepts.exampleLine: He was short of the marker by an inch.

concepts.definition: A fresh set of four downs, earned by gaining 10 yards or more.
concepts.exampleLine: That is a first down. Four more tries.

concepts.definition: The count of the current try and yards still needed, said like third and seven.
concepts.exampleLine: Third and seven, they have to throw.

concepts.definition: Sixty minutes of playing time in four quarters. The clock stops often, so games take about three hours.
concepts.exampleLine: They are just trying to run out the clock.

concepts.definition: The 40-second countdown (25 after some stoppages) to snap the ball. Miss it and it is delay of game.
concepts.exampleLine: Snap it! The play clock is dying.

concepts.definition: A pause each team can call, three per half, to stop the clock and regroup.
concepts.exampleLine: He burned a timeout just to think.

concepts.definition: Six points for getting the ball into the end zone, by carrying it in or catching it there.
concepts.exampleLine: Touchdown! Six points and a shot at the extra one.

concepts.definition: Three points for kicking the ball through the uprights, usually on fourth down.
concepts.exampleLine: Just take the three and kick the field goal.

concepts.definition: One point for a kick after a touchdown, snapped from the 15-yard line (a 33-yard kick).
concepts.exampleLine: The extra point is good, seven total.

concepts.definition: After a touchdown, run or pass it in from the 2-yard line for two points instead of kicking.
concepts.exampleLine: They are going for two. Bold.

concepts.definition: Two points for the defense when the offense is tackled in its own end zone. The scorers also get the ball back.
concepts.exampleLine: A safety! Two points and we get the ball.

concepts.definition: When the offense loses the ball to the defense by interception or fumble.
concepts.exampleLine: That turnover flipped the whole game.

concepts.definition: A pass caught by a defender. The defense takes over the ball.
concepts.exampleLine: He got picked off. He never saw the linebacker.

concepts.definition: The ball carrier loses control of the ball. Either team can recover it.
concepts.exampleLine: Fumble! The ball is loose, who has it?

concepts.definition: A kick on fourth down that sends the ball to the other team as far downfield as possible.
concepts.exampleLine: They punted. It was fourth and long anyway.

concepts.definition: One offensive possession from getting the ball until scoring, punting or turning it over.
concepts.exampleLine: That was a 14-play, seven-minute drive.

concepts.definition: Which team has the ball. The other team is on defense.
concepts.exampleLine: We finally have possession again.

concepts.definition: The player who runs the offense: takes the snap, then throws or hands off.
concepts.exampleLine: Their quarterback looks calm under pressure.

concepts.definition: Lines up behind the quarterback; runs the ball, catches passes, sometimes blocks.
concepts.exampleLine: The running back found a hole.

concepts.definition: Lines up wide and runs routes to catch passes.
concepts.exampleLine: Their number-one receiver is a problem.

concepts.definition: A hybrid who blocks like a lineman and catches like a receiver.
concepts.exampleLine: Tight end is both jobs at once.

concepts.definition: Five big players (center, two guards, two tackles) who block for the run and protect the quarterback.
concepts.exampleLine: The O-line gave him all day to throw.

concepts.definition: The front players (tackles and ends) who rush the passer and stop runs.
concepts.exampleLine: Their D-line is eating us alive.

concepts.definition: Defenders behind the line who stop runs, rush the passer and cover backs and tight ends.
concepts.exampleLine: The linebacker read that play perfectly.

concepts.definition: A defensive back who lines up wide and covers receivers.
concepts.exampleLine: Their corner is glued to him.

concepts.definition: The deepest defenders, the last line against big plays. Free safety and strong safety.
concepts.exampleLine: Our safeties keep biting on the fake.

concepts.definition: The defensive backs: cornerbacks and safeties who cover receivers.
concepts.exampleLine: Our secondary is getting torched.

concepts.definition: Kickoffs, punts, field goals and returns: the third phase of the game.
concepts.exampleLine: Special teams cost us that game.

concepts.definition: The players allowed to catch a forward pass: backs, receivers and tight ends, identified by number and alignment.
concepts.exampleLine: He was not eligible, so it is a penalty.

concepts.definition: Numbers loosely signal position groups, for example quarterbacks 1-19 and linemen 50-79.
concepts.exampleLine: Number 87 must be a tight end or receiver.

concepts.definition: The head coach runs the team; the offensive (OC) and defensive coordinator (DC) design and often call the plays.
concepts.exampleLine: Fire the offensive coordinator, that play call was awful.

concepts.definition: A ranking of players at each position: starters, then backups.
concepts.exampleLine: He is second on the depth chart now.

concepts.definition: The safety who lines up on the tight end side and helps against the run and short passes.
concepts.exampleLine: The strong safety came up to stop the run.

concepts.definition: How the 11 offensive players line up before the snap.
concepts.exampleLine: Five wide, empty backfield. They are throwing.

concepts.definition: A two-digit code: running backs first, then tight ends. 11 means one back, one tight end, three receivers.
concepts.exampleLine: They are in 11 personnel, three receivers.

concepts.definition: The quarterback lines up several yards behind the center. Common on passing downs.
concepts.exampleLine: Shotgun on third and long. Pass.

concepts.definition: The quarterback takes the snap directly from the center. Common for runs and play-action.
concepts.exampleLine: Under center on third and one. Sneak?

concepts.definition: The menu of pass routes, numbered by depth and break angle: slant, out, curl, post, corner, go.
concepts.exampleLine: Slant, post, corner. It is all the route tree.

concepts.definition: A quick diagonal cut toward the middle after one to three steps.
concepts.exampleLine: Quick slant for the first down.

concepts.definition: A straight sprint down the field; the deep shot.
concepts.exampleLine: He is just running a go, throw it up.

concepts.definition: Run about 8 to 10 yards, then cut sharply to the sideline.
concepts.exampleLine: Out route to the sideline to stop the clock.

concepts.definition: Run deep, then cut diagonally toward the goalposts.
concepts.exampleLine: The post was wide open.

concepts.definition: Run downfield, then turn back toward the quarterback to settle in a gap.
concepts.exampleLine: He sat down in the zone on a curl.

concepts.definition: A short pass behind the line with blockers set up in front, meant to punish an aggressive rush.
concepts.exampleLine: The screen killed their blitz.

concepts.definition: Fake a handoff, then throw. It freezes linebackers and opens space behind them.
concepts.exampleLine: Play-action fooled the whole defense.

concepts.definition: One snap, and the quarterback chooses to hand off or throw after reading one defender.
concepts.exampleLine: That RPO puts the linebacker in a bind.

concepts.definition: A player moves before the snap to reveal the coverage or create a mismatch.
concepts.exampleLine: Watch the motion. The corner followed him, so it is man.

concepts.definition: The quarterback changes the play at the line after reading the defense.
concepts.exampleLine: He audibled out of that play.

concepts.definition: Skipping the huddle to speed up tempo and limit defensive substitutions.
concepts.exampleLine: They went no-huddle and gassed the defense.

concepts.definition: A receiver changes his route on the fly, usually to beat a blitz.
concepts.exampleLine: Hot route to the slant, that is a beaten blitz.

concepts.definition: A safe short throw to the running back when the deeper options are covered.
concepts.exampleLine: He took the checkdown. Fine, not exciting.

concepts.definition: Four defensive linemen and three linebackers.
concepts.exampleLine: They are in a base 4-3.

concepts.definition: Three linemen and four linebackers, with the extra linebackers rushing from the edge.
concepts.exampleLine: In a 3-4 the outside linebackers are the pass rushers.

concepts.definition: Each defender shadows one receiver wherever he goes.
concepts.exampleLine: If it is man, the corner follows him everywhere.

concepts.definition: Defenders guard areas of the field instead of specific players.
concepts.exampleLine: They are in zone, so sit down in the hole.

concepts.definition: The core coverage distinction: guard an area, or guard a person. Everything else builds on it.
concepts.exampleLine: Is that man or zone? I could not tell.

concepts.definition: Man coverage with no deep safety help, usually paired with an all-out blitz. High risk, high reward.
concepts.exampleLine: Cover 0 means one miss is a touchdown.

concepts.definition: Man coverage underneath with one deep safety (single-high).
concepts.exampleLine: One deep safety, that is Cover 1.

concepts.definition: Two safeties split the deep field into halves while corners guard the flats. The hole is between corner and safety.
concepts.exampleLine: They are in Cover 2, so throw to the seam.

concepts.definition: A zone where three defenders split the deep field into thirds.
concepts.exampleLine: They are sitting in Cover 3 and giving up the short stuff.

concepts.definition: Also called quarters: four defenders each take a deep quarter of the field.
concepts.exampleLine: Quarters is why nobody got behind them.

concepts.definition: Sending more than the usual four pass rushers, often a linebacker or defensive back.
concepts.exampleLine: He blitzed and got home.

concepts.definition: The defensive line and rushers attacking the quarterback.
concepts.exampleLine: Their pass rush is the reason we lost.

concepts.definition: Tackling the quarterback behind the line of scrimmage for a loss of yards.
concepts.exampleLine: Sack! That is second and long now.

concepts.definition: Hurrying or hitting the quarterback, even without a sack. Fans and analysts track pressure rate.
concepts.exampleLine: He was under pressure all night.

concepts.definition: Five defensive backs, the standard answer to three-receiver sets.
concepts.exampleLine: Nickel is basically their base defense now.

concepts.definition: A corner lines up right on the receiver and jams him at the line.
concepts.exampleLine: Press coverage, the corner is in his face.

concepts.definition: The spaces between blockers (A between center and guard, B guard to tackle, C outside the tackle) that defenders are assigned to fill.
concepts.exampleLine: The linebacker lost his gap and the back got out.

concepts.definition: Showing one coverage before the snap and rotating into another after.
concepts.exampleLine: They disguised it beautifully, looked like Cover 2 and turned into Cover 3.

concepts.definition: An outside pass rusher, among the most valuable players on defense.
concepts.exampleLine: Their edge rusher is a monster.

concepts.definition: Two rushers swap lanes to confuse the blockers.
concepts.exampleLine: That stunt freed up the guy inside.

concepts.definition: A defender is across the line of scrimmage when the ball is snapped. Five yards.
concepts.exampleLine: Offside on the defense, five yards.

concepts.definition: An offensive player moves before the snap, and the play is dead. Five yards.
concepts.exampleLine: False start again? Their tackle is jumpy.

concepts.definition: Illegally grabbing a player. Ten yards on offense; five yards and an automatic first down on defense.
concepts.exampleLine: That was holding, ten yards, brings it back.

concepts.definition: Illegal contact with a receiver before the ball arrives. In the NFL it is a spot foul.
concepts.exampleLine: That should have been pass interference.

concepts.definition: An illegal hit on the quarterback: 15 yards and an automatic first down.
concepts.exampleLine: Roughing the passer is a free first down.

concepts.definition: College penalty: forcible contact to the head or neck of a defenseless player. Ejection when confirmed.
concepts.exampleLine: They reviewed it for targeting, that is an ejection.

concepts.definition: A tackle where the defender swivels his hips and drops his weight onto the runner's legs. Banned by the NFL from 2024.
concepts.exampleLine: That is a hip-drop, fifteen yards.

concepts.definition: Throwing the ball away with no receiver nearby to dodge a sack. Loss of down and yardage.
concepts.exampleLine: That is intentional grounding, no one was near it.

concepts.definition: The offense fails to snap before the play clock hits zero. Five yards.
concepts.exampleLine: Delay of game. They lost track of the clock.

concepts.definition: A receiver must control the ball, get both feet (or another body part) down inbounds, and make a football move.
concepts.exampleLine: Was that a catch? The rule is so confusing.

concepts.definition: Scoring plays and turnovers are automatically reviewed; coaches can challenge other calls with a red flag.
concepts.exampleLine: He threw the red flag. He is challenging it.

concepts.definition: The team that did not commit the foul may accept the penalty or decline it and keep the play result.
concepts.exampleLine: They declined the penalty because the play was better.

concepts.definition: The offense must have seven players on the line of scrimmage and only certain players may be eligible receivers.
concepts.exampleLine: Illegal formation, they only had six on the line.

concepts.definition: A kick that starts each half and follows every score.
concepts.exampleLine: Kickoff to start the second half.

concepts.definition: The modern kickoff: the kicking team lines up at the receiving team's 40, with a setup zone and a landing zone to create more returns and fewer injuries.
concepts.exampleLine: The new kickoff is why returns are back.

concepts.definition: The ball is dead in the end zone and the receiving team starts at a set spot: the 35 after a kickoff (2025 rule), the 20 after a punt.
concepts.exampleLine: He took the touchback, starts at the 35.

concepts.definition: The returner waves an arm, cannot be hit, and cannot run the ball back.
concepts.exampleLine: He signaled for a fair catch.

concepts.definition: A short kick the kicking team tries to recover. Since 2026 a team can declare one at any time.
concepts.exampleLine: They are trying an onside kick, this is desperate.

concepts.definition: Roughly inside the opponent's 35, where a kicker makes most attempts. Attempt length is about 17 yards more than the yard line.
concepts.exampleLine: That is 55 yards, that is a long field goal.

concepts.definition: A punt aimed out of bounds near the goal line so the returner cannot use it.
concepts.exampleLine: Great coffin-corner punt.

concepts.definition: Go for it, punt or kick a field goal. The most argued choice in football.
concepts.exampleLine: Go for it! Why did he punt?

concepts.definition: Inside the opponent's 20-yard line, where the field shrinks and scoring gets harder.
concepts.exampleLine: We stall every time in the red zone.

concepts.definition: The make-or-break down. Convert and the drive lives; fail and it is a punt or fourth-down gamble.
concepts.exampleLine: The defense needs one stop on third down.

concepts.definition: The hurry-up offense before halftime or the end of the game, saving the clock with sideline throws and timeouts.
concepts.exampleLine: Two-minute drill, can they get a field goal?

concepts.definition: Using timeouts, out-of-bounds plays and running plays to control how much time is left.
concepts.exampleLine: Awful clock management, he left time on the clock.

concepts.definition: The kneel-down: the quarterback takes the snap and drops to a knee to run out the clock.
concepts.exampleLine: They are kneeling. Game over.

concepts.definition: Extra period when tied. NFL regular season: 10 minutes, and since 2025 both teams get a possession like the playoffs.
concepts.exampleLine: Overtime! Both teams get the ball now.

concepts.definition: Two conferences (AFC and NFC), four divisions each, four teams per division. Division rivals play twice a year.
concepts.exampleLine: That is a division game, it matters more.

concepts.definition: Each team plays 17 games over 18 weeks with one bye week.
concepts.exampleLine: Seventeen games, plus one bye.

concepts.definition: Seven teams per conference: four division winners then three wild cards. Only the number-one seed gets a first-round bye.
concepts.exampleLine: We need the number-one seed for the bye.

concepts.definition: Seven rounds each April where teams select college players, worst records picking first.
concepts.exampleLine: Bad team, top pick. That is the draft.

concepts.definition: The league-wide limit on what a team can spend on player salaries.
concepts.exampleLine: They are cap-strapped so they cut him.

concepts.definition: Players whose contracts ended can sign with any team, opening each March.
concepts.exampleLine: He hit free agency and signed for a fortune.

concepts.definition: A one-year, high-salary contract a team can force on a key player to keep him.
concepts.exampleLine: They franchise-tagged him rather than lose him.

concepts.definition: Extra players a team keeps for practice who can be signed to the active roster.
concepts.exampleLine: He was on the practice squad and got called up.

concepts.definition: A list for injured players who miss at least several weeks and free up a roster spot.
concepts.exampleLine: He is on IR for the year.

concepts.definition: The active roster: 53 players, of whom 48 dress for a game.
concepts.exampleLine: They cut down to 53.

concepts.definition: The date after which teams cannot make trades until the new league year.
concepts.exampleLine: Trade deadline is Tuesday, watch for a move.

concepts.definition: The week off in the schedule, plus a chance to rest and heal.
concepts.exampleLine: Bye week, so no game to stress about.

concepts.definition: A game where fans draft real players and score points from their real stats each week.
concepts.exampleLine: My fantasy team needs a big week from him.

concepts.definition: Nationally televised night games: Thursday, Sunday and Monday night.
concepts.exampleLine: Sunday Night Football is our game this week.

concepts.definition: Linemen block an area together and the back picks his hole, rather than each having a specific target.
concepts.exampleLine: Zone blocking is why he cut back.

concepts.definition: Blocking where each lineman has an assigned gap, often with a puller leading the way: power and counter.
concepts.exampleLine: Power is a gap scheme, a guard pulls.

concepts.definition: A lineman who steps back and runs across the formation to lead block.
concepts.exampleLine: The pulling guard cleared the corner.

concepts.definition: The staple run: the back reads the blockers and takes the first crease, mainly between the tackles.
concepts.exampleLine: Inside zone up the middle again.

concepts.definition: The back stretches the play sideways, then plants and cuts upfield through a lane.
concepts.exampleLine: Outside zone, stretch it, then cut.

concepts.definition: How the line and backs divide up the rushers: man, zone-slide, or a mix. The center calls the protection.
concepts.exampleLine: The center pointed out the Mike.

concepts.definition: What the quarterback identifies before the snap: safeties, corner leverage, box count, and blitz threats.
concepts.exampleLine: He saw the blitz pre-snap and changed it.

concepts.definition: Two or more routes designed to beat a coverage together, like mesh, flood, or smash.
concepts.exampleLine: That flood concept overloaded the zone.

concepts.definition: The order in which the quarterback checks receivers: first read, second read, checkdown.
concepts.exampleLine: He went through his progression and found the third read.

concepts.definition: The gap between defenders where the ball can be completed. It opens and closes in tenths of a second.
concepts.exampleLine: The window was tiny but he threaded it.

concepts.definition: Throwing before the receiver breaks, to where he will be, to beat the defender.
concepts.exampleLine: That anticipation throw was perfect.

concepts.definition: A throw placed on the receiver's back shoulder so only he can catch it against tight coverage.
concepts.exampleLine: Back-shoulder throw, the corner had no play.

concepts.definition: Yards gained after the reception; a mark of a dangerous receiver.
concepts.exampleLine: He gets so many yards after catch.

concepts.definition: A quick surge behind the center by the quarterback on short yardage, including the tush push.
concepts.exampleLine: The tush push is just a quarterback sneak with a shove.

concepts.definition: A timing-based passing system using short, quick throws as a substitute for runs. Bill Walsh popularized it.
concepts.exampleLine: It is a West Coast offense, lots of short passes.

concepts.definition: A pass-heavy system with spread formations and simple, repeated concepts. Mike Leach and Hal Mumme.
concepts.exampleLine: College Air Raid is why teams throw 50 times.

concepts.definition: The Shanahan tree offense: outside zone, then play-action off the same look.
concepts.exampleLine: The Shanahan offense looks like zone, then a bootleg.

concepts.definition: A zone that turns into man once receivers enter an area. Modern defense blends both.
concepts.exampleLine: It looks like zone but it is really match coverage.

concepts.definition: A Cover 2 where the middle linebacker drops deep to cover the hole between the safeties.
concepts.exampleLine: The Tampa 2 is why they beat the deep pass.

concepts.definition: Rush a linebacker or defensive back while a lineman drops into coverage.
concepts.exampleLine: They zone-blitzed, the lineman dropped back.

concepts.definition: Two safeties deep before the snap, either Cover 2, Cover 4, or a disguise.
concepts.exampleLine: Two-high, so run it.

concepts.definition: One deep safety before the snap: Cover 1 or Cover 3.
concepts.exampleLine: Single-high means they are stacking the box.

concepts.definition: Fewer than seven defenders near the line of scrimmage, so running is easier.
concepts.exampleLine: They are in a light box, hand it off.

concepts.definition: A player facing an opponent he is much better against, such as a fast tight end on a linebacker.
concepts.exampleLine: They found a mismatch with the tight end.

concepts.definition: A stat measuring how much each play changes the team's expected scoring. Positive helps.
concepts.exampleLine: His EPA per play is elite.

concepts.definition: The share of plays that keep the offense on schedule: about 40 percent of needed yards on first down, 60 on second, all on third.
concepts.exampleLine: Success rate says the offense is fine.

concepts.definition: The argument over whether running backs are worth big contracts given short careers and easy replacement.
concepts.exampleLine: Paying a running back that much? That is the whole debate.

concepts.definition: Crediting the quarterback with the team's record; a widely disputed stat.
concepts.exampleLine: Quarterback wins is not a real stat.

concepts.definition: Whether the kickoff is too dangerous to keep, and how far to change it, versus tradition.
concepts.exampleLine: The kickoff debate never ends.

concepts.definition: Whether the shove-assisted quarterback sneak should be banned. A 2025 vote failed 22-10, short of the 24 needed.
concepts.exampleLine: The tush push is unfair, or unstoppable?

concepts.definition: The league procedure to remove and clear players after a suspected head injury.
concepts.exampleLine: He is in the concussion protocol, he is out.

concepts.definition: A desperate long pass into a crowded end zone, usually as time expires.
concepts.exampleLine: That Hail Mary was pure luck.

concepts.definition: The NFL championship game, held each February since the 1966 season. The winner takes the Lombardi Trophy.
concepts.exampleLine: They are in the Super Bowl this year.

concepts.definition: The 1966 agreement combining two rival leagues, creating the conferences and the Super Bowl.
concepts.exampleLine: The AFC used to be the AFL.

concepts.definition: A team that dominates for years, such as the 1970s Steelers or the 2000s-2010s Patriots.
concepts.exampleLine: Dynasty talk always starts with the Patriots.

concepts.definition: The famous plays fans reference: the Immaculate Reception, the Catch, the Helmet Catch, the Philly Special.
concepts.exampleLine: Everyone brings up the Immaculate Reception.

concepts.definition: The Pro Football Hall of Fame in Canton, Ohio; its yearly class is a big argument each February.
concepts.exampleLine: He is a first-ballot Hall of Famer.

concepts.definition: Each team gets the ball at the opponent's 25 for one untimed possession in alternating rounds; from the third round, two-point tries only.
concepts.exampleLine: College overtime is just a shootout.

concepts.definition: The clock stops on a first down only briefly; the college clock also stops after incomplete passes and out of bounds.
concepts.exampleLine: In college the clock runs more.

concepts.definition: A college receiver needs only one foot inbounds, not two.
concepts.exampleLine: It is one foot in college, two in the NFL.

concepts.definition: The ongoing reshuffling of college conferences, with the SEC and Big Ten now dominant.
concepts.exampleLine: Realignment ruined the old rivalries.

concepts.definition: A 12-team playoff: four conference champions and the highest-ranked Group of 6 champion get bids, top four seeds get byes.
concepts.exampleLine: We need to finish in the top four for the bye.

concepts.definition: The system that lets college players transfer freely and immediately; rosters turn over every year.
concepts.exampleLine: Half his roster is new from the portal.

concepts.definition: Name, image and likeness deals, and since 2025 direct revenue sharing, paying college athletes.
concepts.exampleLine: NIL is why the best players stay in school.

concepts.definition: The annual award for the most outstanding player in college football.
concepts.exampleLine: He is a Heisman contender.

concepts.definition: Postseason college games; the biggest are New Year's Six bowls and the playoff.
concepts.exampleLine: Bowl season is just football all December.

concepts.definition: Weekly rankings (AP poll, Coaches poll, and the playoff committee) that shape the playoff race.
concepts.exampleLine: We dropped in the rankings after that loss.

concepts.definition: A yearly game with deep history where records do not matter: Ohio State-Michigan, Iron Bowl, Army-Navy.
concepts.exampleLine: In a rivalry game you throw out the records.

concepts.definition: How colleges land high school players, ranked with stars, with national signing days.
concepts.exampleLine: Their recruiting class is the best in the country.

concepts.definition: What a team is known for: its scheme, star players and fan culture. Personalized per team.
concepts.exampleLine: What is your team's whole identity?

concepts.definition: The three teams in your division that you play twice each year.
concepts.exampleLine: Beat your divisional rivals or forget the playoffs.

concepts.definition: Pre-game parties in the parking lot, with food, music and games. A core fan ritual.
concepts.exampleLine: I will bring a cooler to the tailgate.

concepts.definition: The weekly official listing of who is out, doubtful, questionable or full-participation.
concepts.exampleLine: He is listed as questionable, so who knows.

concepts.definition: Who is in, who is out and what each team needs, updated weekly.
concepts.exampleLine: We need the tiebreaker to get in.

concepts.definition: The rules to rank teams with equal records: head-to-head, division record and more.
concepts.exampleLine: We win the head-to-head tiebreaker.

concepts.definition: Media rankings of teams by current strength rather than record.
concepts.exampleLine: We are third in the power rankings.

concepts.definition: The yearly rules tweaks approved each spring. Includes the 2026 kickoff and officiating changes.
concepts.exampleLine: The new kickoff rule changes things.

concepts.definition: A specific, curious question that shows you listened and want to learn more.
concepts.exampleLine: Why do you think the defense keeps collapsing on third down?

concepts.definition: Respond to what they said before adding your own opinion; the base skill of good conversation.
concepts.exampleLine: Wait, tell me what you saw on that play.

concepts.definition: Admit what you do not know and ask. Faking expertise is easy to spot and loses trust.
concepts.exampleLine: I do not know that term, teach me?

units.title: The basics
units.summary: The goal, the field, the clock, four downs and how scoring works.

lessons.title: What the game is about
lessons.objective: You can say in one sentence how a team wins.

payload.prompt: How many points is a touchdown worth?

explanation.correct: A touchdown is worth 6. Then the team gets a shot at one more (kick) or two more (run or pass).
explanation.incorrect: A touchdown is six points. The seven-point thing happens after: kick for one, or two-point try for two.

payload.prompt: What do you need to do to score a touchdown?

options.text: Get the ball into the end zone

explanation.correct: Get the ball into the end zone by carrying it or catching it there. Six points every time.
explanation.incorrect: The end zone is the goal. Carry it in, catch it in, or even recover a fumble in it. That is a touchdown.
explanation.sayThisLine: He is in the end zone!

payload.prompt: Tap the end zone where the offense wants to go.

scene.alt: A football field from above. The end zones are at each end, 10 yards deep.

explanation.correct: The end zone is the 10-yard area at the far end. Score there and it is a touchdown.
explanation.incorrect: The end zone is at the far end of the field. That is where you want to go.

payload.prompt: She says: 'Did we get in?'

replies.text: Yeah, touchdown!
replies.theirResponse: Nice! So we got six?
replies.coachNote: Short and right. She will explain the extra point.

replies.text: I'm not sure if he had both feet in.
replies.theirResponse: Good question, they probably will review it.
replies.coachNote: Smart. Admitting doubt shows you are paying attention.

replies.text: That was definitely not a catch.
replies.theirResponse: Wait, he was running the ball, not catching it.
replies.coachNote: Oops. A ball carrier just needs to get in, not both feet down.

lessons.title: The field and the line
lessons.objective: You can point to the end zone, yard lines and the line of scrimmage.

payload.prompt: Tap the line of scrimmage (where the offense snaps the ball).

scene.alt: Top-down view of the line of scrimmage with offense lined up.

explanation.correct: The line of scrimmage is where the ball sits. Nobody crosses it until the snap.
explanation.incorrect: The line of scrimmage is the exact line the ball is on. That is where play starts.

payload.prompt: Complete the sentence.
payload.template: The field is {{length}} yards long, plus a {{zone}} at each end.

explanation.correct: 100-yard field plus two 10-yard end zones = 120 total. The end zones are where you score.
explanation.incorrect: The playing field is 100 yards. Each end zone is 10 yards deep, that is where touchdowns happen.

payload.prompt: What does field position mean in football?

options.text: Where the ball is on the field
How many yards each team gains

explanation.correct: Field position is where the ball sits. Close to the opponent's end zone is good; close to your own is dangerous.
explanation.incorrect: Field position is about the ball's location. The closer you are to scoring, the better your field position.

payload.prompt: She says: 'How do they know if it is a new set of downs?'

replies.text: They use the yellow line on TV. Ten yards from the line of scrimmage.
replies.theirResponse: Ohhh, so that is what that thing is for.
replies.coachNote: Perfect. You explained something she did not know. That is what this is about.

replies.text: I'm not really sure.
replies.theirResponse: OK, it is just the chains on the field. Ten yards from where the ball was.
replies.coachNote: Honest is OK. You can both learn together.

replies.text: The ref just decides randomly.
replies.theirResponse: That doesn't sound right...
replies.coachNote: Not the move. The chains measure exactly 10 yards.

lessons.title: Four downs
lessons.objective: You can explain what a down is and why fourth down matters.

payload.prompt: How many downs does the offense get to gain 10 yards?

explanation.correct: Four tries to move 10 yards. Gain them and the count resets to first down.
explanation.incorrect: It is four downs. Most teams punt on fourth down instead of gambling.
explanation.sayThisLine: They have four downs to get 10 yards.

payload.prompt: What does a first down give the offense?

explanation.correct: Gain 10 yards and the count resets: four fresh tries. That is why fans cheer a first down.
explanation.incorrect: A first down resets the offense to four tries at another 10 yards. It is not points or timeouts, just more time with the ball.
explanation.sayThisLine: They picked up the first down.

payload.prompt: They gained 6 yards on second down with 8 yards to go. What is the next down and distance?

explanation.correct: They needed 8, gained 6, so 2 yards left. Third and two.
explanation.incorrect: Subtract what they gained from what they needed. Needed 8, got 6, so third and two remains.
explanation.sayThisLine: Third and two. They have to get this.

payload.prompt: She says: 'Why does everyone care about fourth down so much?'

replies.text: Because it is the last chance. Either they get it or lose the ball.
replies.theirResponse: Oh! So you have to decide whether to gamble or punt.
replies.coachNote: Nailed it. Fourth down is the most dramatic moment in football.

replies.text: It is just a big deal, I guess?
replies.theirResponse: Yeah it is, but I am not sure why.
replies.coachNote: A chance to bond over learning together. Ask what she has seen happen on fourth down.

replies.text: I don't know, there are only four of them.
replies.theirResponse: Well, there are always four downs...
replies.coachNote: Not quite. The point is that fourth is the last one: succeed or lose the ball.

lessons.title: Where is the first down?
lessons.objective: You can read the yellow line and say if they got the first down.

payload.prompt: The ball is spotted at the 47-yard line. The yellow marker is at the 57-yard line. Did they get the first down?

explanation.correct: 57 minus 47 is 10 yards. Exactly at the marker means the first down stands.
explanation.incorrect: The yellow line shows where 10 yards is. At the 47 you need the 57 to get a new set of downs.

payload.prompt: Started at the 23-yard line. Yellow marker at the 33-yard line. They reach the 32-yard line. First down?

explanation.correct: The marker is at 33. The ball is at 32. One yard short of the first down.
explanation.incorrect: Need to reach the yellow line or go past it. Being one yard short means the chain is used and it is close.
explanation.sayThisLine: He is short of the marker.

payload.prompt: Tap where the offense needs to reach to get a new set of downs.

scene.alt: Overhead view. Offense lines up at the left, yellow marker 10 yards to the right.

explanation.correct: Exactly at the yellow line or beyond it and you get a fresh set of downs.
explanation.incorrect: The yellow marker shows where first down is. Reach it or go past it.
explanation.sayThisLine: The chains are out for a measurement.

payload.prompt: She says: 'Is the yellow line always there?'

replies.text: On TV yes. On the field they use the chains to measure if it is close.
replies.theirResponse: Ohhh, so they bring out the chains sometimes?
replies.coachNote: Exactly right. TV adds the yellow for us; the field uses actual chains.

replies.text: I think so? I'm not totally sure.
replies.theirResponse: I've seen them measure before when it was really close.
replies.coachNote: You can ask: 'So they need to measure it?' and keep learning together.

replies.text: It is just drawn by the refs with a laser.
replies.theirResponse: A laser? That doesn't sound real.
replies.coachNote: Not how it works. Real chains on the field, and a computer line for TV viewers.

lessons.title: The clock
lessons.objective: You can say how long a game is and why it feels longer.

payload.prompt: How many minutes of actual playing time are there in a football game?

explanation.correct: Four 15-minute quarters = 60 minutes of play time. But the clock stops constantly, so games last three hours.
explanation.incorrect: Sixty minutes total, split into four 15-minute quarters. That is why a game takes three hours even though it is only one hour of play.
explanation.sayThisLine: There's only 10 minutes left in the game.

payload.prompt: What is the play clock?

options.text: How long the refs have to throw a flag
The countdown to snap the ball (40 or 25 seconds)
The time left in the quarter

explanation.correct: The offense has 40 seconds (or 25 after certain stoppages) to snap the ball. Hit zero and it is delay of game.
explanation.incorrect: The play clock is the countdown to the snap. Offense has to line up and go. 40 seconds most plays, 25 after a timeout or penalty.
explanation.sayThisLine: The play clock is running out!

payload.prompt: How many timeouts does each team get per half?

explanation.correct: Three timeouts per half. Six total per game (three in each half). Teams use them to stop the clock and regroup.
explanation.incorrect: Each team gets three per half, so six in a game. That is when they can stop the clock and talk strategy.

payload.prompt: Tap the button when the play clock hits zero. (Delay of game!)

explanation.correct: You caught the delay of game. Five-yard penalty.
explanation.early: A bit early. The play clock was still going.
explanation.late: Too late, the penalty was already called.
explanation.incorrect: Timing is tight. The offense has to snap before zero.

lessons.title: How points happen
lessons.objective: You can add up a score from touchdowns, kicks and safeties.

payload.prompt: Match each score type to its points.

explanation.correct: Touchdown 6, field goal 3, extra point 1, two-point try 2. Adding them up is how you follow the score.
explanation.incorrect: Remember: TD is six, not seven. The extra point comes after.

payload.prompt: In the NFL, where does a two-point try start?

explanation.correct: The NFL uses the 2-yard line. College snaps from the 3, one of the small differences between the two games.
explanation.incorrect: The NFL snaps two-point tries from the 2-yard line. College uses the 3-yard line, so the two versions feel slightly different.
explanation.sayThisLine: Going for two from the two-yard line is a coin flip.

payload.prompt: A kicker is 52 yards away from the goal line. How far is that field goal attempt (roughly)?

explanation.correct: Field goal range is about yard line plus 17 yards. So 52 plus 17 is 69 yards.
explanation.incorrect: A 52-yard attempt is roughly 69 total (the yard line plus 17 for snapper, holder, kick arc). That is a long one.

payload.prompt: Score so far: TD + kick (6+1), then FG. What is the total?

explanation.correct: Touchdown (6) + extra point (1) + field goal (3) = 10 points.
explanation.incorrect: Six for the touchdown, one for the kick, three for the field goal. That adds up to 10.

lessons.title: Giving the ball away
lessons.objective: You can say the difference between a fumble, an interception and a punt.

payload.prompt: Match the turnover type to its description.

options.text: Ball carrier loses control of the ball

explanation.correct: Interception is caught, fumble is lost. Either way, the other team gets the ball.
explanation.incorrect: An interception is when a defender catches a pass. A fumble is when a ball carrier loses it.

payload.prompt: What is a punt?

options.text: A forced handoff on fourth down
A kick on fourth down that gives the ball to the other team
A penalty for hitting too hard

explanation.correct: A punt is a kick on fourth down. The offense voluntarily gives the ball to the other team but moves it downfield.
explanation.incorrect: Punting is not giving up; it is a strategic move. Send the ball far away so the other team starts way downfield.
explanation.sayThisLine: They should have punted from there.

payload.prompt: Put these in order: a drive ends, the offense turns it over, the other team gets the ball.

explanation.correct: The turnover happens, the drive ends, and the other team takes possession.
explanation.incorrect: When a turnover happens, the drive is over and the other team starts with the ball from that spot.

payload.prompt: She says: 'Did we pick that off?'

replies.text: Yeah, interception! We got the ball.
replies.theirResponse: Yes! Whose ball is it now?
replies.coachNote: Perfect. An interception is a turnover, we now have possession.

replies.text: I think so, it was close though.
replies.theirResponse: Close enough for a flag review I bet.
replies.coachNote: Good instinct. Close plays do get reviewed.

replies.text: It was a fumble, not an interception.
replies.theirResponse: Wait, he threw it, so it has to be an interception.
replies.coachNote: True story: if it is thrown and caught by a defender, it is an interception, not a fumble.

units.title: Who does what
units.summary: Every position on the field and what fans mean when they name one.

lessons.title: The quarterback
lessons.objective: You can say why everyone talks about the quarterback.

payload.prompt: What is the quarterback's main job?

options.text: Kick the ball through the uprights
Run the offense: take the snap and throw or hand off
Call out the defense before every play

explanation.correct: The QB is the engine of the offense. He takes the snap, reads the defense and throws or hands off.
explanation.incorrect: Everything runs through the quarterback. That is why fans obsess over who plays the position.
explanation.sayThisLine: Their quarterback is having a great game.

payload.prompt: Who designs the plays the quarterback runs?

options.text: The offensive coordinator, working with the head coach

explanation.correct: The offensive coordinator (OC) designs plays and calls them. The head coach oversees everything.
explanation.incorrect: When fans complain about a play call, they usually mean the offensive coordinator made a bad choice.
explanation.sayThisLine: That is a terrible play call by the OC.

payload.prompt: She says: 'Why do they always blame the quarterback?'

replies.text: Because he is the center of the offense. Every play goes through him.
replies.theirResponse: Oh, so if things go wrong it is his fault?
replies.coachNote: Smart. QB gets credit and blame because he is that important.

replies.text: I'm not sure, but he is definitely the star.
replies.theirResponse: I guess that makes sense.
replies.coachNote: True. QB is usually the biggest name on the team.

replies.text: It is kind of unfair, the whole team plays.
replies.theirResponse: Yeah, but he is kind of the leader.
replies.coachNote: True, the whole team matters. But the QB sets the tone for the offense.

lessons.title: Backs, receivers and tight ends
lessons.objective: You can tell the skill positions apart by what they do.

payload.prompt: Match each position to what they do.

options.text: Runs the ball and catches short passes
Lines up wide and catches passes downfield
Blocks like a lineman, catches like a receiver

explanation.correct: RB runs it or catches it. WR catches and runs routes. TE is both a blocker and a receiver.
explanation.incorrect: These three are the main skill positions. They catch passes and/or run the ball.

payload.prompt: Is this formation 11 personnel or 12 personnel?

scene.alt: Offensive formation with one RB in backfield, one TE, and three receivers wide.

explanation.correct: 11 means one back, one tight end, three receivers. That is a pass-heavy formation.
explanation.incorrect: The code is running backs first, then tight ends. 11 = one and one.

payload.prompt: She says: 'What is a tight end? Like, why is he tight?'

replies.text: He lines up tight to the tackle, so he is close, not split out wide like a receiver.
replies.theirResponse: Ohhh, that is where the name comes from!
replies.coachNote: Exactly right. The name comes from his alignment.

replies.text: He is like a receiver but bigger and stronger.
replies.theirResponse: So he can block better?
replies.coachNote: Good instinct. That is part of it.

replies.text: I have no idea, it is a weird name.
replies.theirResponse: Maybe we will find out eventually.
replies.coachNote: Honest is good. And now you know: tight end = aligned tight to the tackle.

lessons.title: The big guys up front
lessons.objective: You can explain what the offensive line is protecting and why fans love a good one.

payload.prompt: How many players make up the offensive line?

explanation.correct: Five: center, two guards and two tackles. They block for the run and protect the passer.
explanation.incorrect: The offensive line is the five big guys up front: center, guards and tackles.

payload.prompt: Tap the offensive line (the five blockers in front).

scene.alt: Top view showing the offensive line at the line of scrimmage.

explanation.correct: The offensive line lines up at the line of scrimmage. They are the biggest guys who block.
explanation.incorrect: The O-line is right at the line, ready to block. Center snaps it and they go.

payload.prompt: She says: 'Why do fans care so much about the offensive line?'

replies.text: Because good blocking changes everything. Gives the QB time and the RB running lanes.
replies.theirResponse: So if the line is bad, the whole offense is bad?
replies.coachNote: Exactly. A great line hides a mediocre QB or RB.

replies.text: They are big and strong and fans respect that.
replies.theirResponse: Fair enough, they are impressive.
replies.coachNote: True, but the deeper thing is that they enable everything else.

replies.text: I'm not sure, is the line important?
replies.theirResponse: Supposedly a lot of people think so.
replies.coachNote: Now you are learning: line play determines if the QB gets sacked or the RB finds holes.

lessons.title: Linebackers and defensive backs
lessons.objective: You can name the defenders behind the line and what each one covers.

payload.prompt: Match each defender to their main role.

options.text: Stop runs and rush the passer from behind the line
Line up wide and cover receivers
Deepest defender, the last line against big plays

explanation.correct: LB is in the middle, CB on the edge covering receivers, S way back as the last line of defense.
explanation.incorrect: Linebackers are the run stoppers and blitzers. Corners cover receivers. Safeties help over the top.

payload.prompt: Tap a safety (the deepest defensive back).

scene.alt: Defensive formation from above. Safeties are at the top (deep), corners on the edges, linebackers in the middle.

explanation.correct: Safeties line up deep to cover the back of the defense. They are the last line.
explanation.incorrect: Safeties are the deepest defenders on the field. They help over the top on deep passes.

payload.prompt: She says: 'The linebacker made a tackle in the backfield, right?'

replies.text: Yes! He got in the backfield and brought down the running back. That is a loss of yards.
replies.theirResponse: So linebackers are the hard hitters?
replies.coachNote: Basically. LBs are the middle of the defense. They stop runs and rush the passer.

replies.text: I think so, it looked like a good play.
replies.theirResponse: Yeah that was cool.
replies.coachNote: A tackle in the backfield is definitely a big play. Show that you understood.

replies.text: I'm not sure what a linebacker is.
replies.theirResponse: He is one of those guys in the middle of the defense.
replies.coachNote: Linebackers are the guys behind the line. They flow to the ball.
